title: Krishna eats the last leaf
hookLine: the pot is empty, a well known for it, angry sage is coming, and Krishna arrives asking for food; why Hindus offer food to God first
carry: a leaf offered with love is enough for God

lines: A SAGE AT THE DOOR, WITH DISCIPLES.
cards: Dinner is over. The plates are washed. The cook has finally sat down and eaten her own meal.
Then there's a knock. A great sage is at the door, with a crowd of disciples behind him, and they would like to be fed. They're going down to the river to bathe first.
They'll be back soon. Hungry. In the forest years of the Mahabharata, this is Draupadi's evening, and the sage is Durvasa, remembered for his temper and his curses.
Today: an empty pot, and the guest who scraped it.

teach.h: A VESSEL THAT FEEDS UNTIL SHE EATS
teach.b: First, the pot. Early in the exile, the sun gives Yudhishthira a vessel that will feed the household and its guests every day, until Draupadi has eaten. So Draupadi serves everyone first and eats last.
Some tellings carry the next part. Duryodhana, hoping to trap his cousins, sends Durvasa at exactly the wrong hour, after Draupadi has eaten. The sage and his disciples go off to bathe.
Draupadi has nothing to give them, and a sage refused hospitality might curse the house.
So she turns to Krishna in her mind, and Krishna arrives. His first words, in paraphrase: I'm hungry. Give me something to eat.
The pot is empty, she tells him; that's why I called you. He asks to see it anyway.
Stuck to the rim is one small scrap of cooked greens, a bit of leaf. Krishna eats it, and says, may this satisfy the one who is the soul of the world.
Down at the river, the sages suddenly feel full, as if they'd eaten a feast, and slip away. Here's the teaching.

teach.h: A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER
teach.b: In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says it plainly, in paraphrase: whoever offers me a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water with love, I accept it.
In this story he shows it: one leaf, from a woman with nothing left, and the soul of the world is satisfied.
That's why, in many Hindu homes, a little of the meal is set before God first, naivedya, and then shared as prasad, blessed food. The size of the offering was never the point.

how: Hindus hear the story of Durvasa's visit in retellings of the Mahabharata and in devotional storytelling; and in many homes a little food is offered to God before the meal, then shared as prasad.

a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water: the love is what he takes.

he eats one bit of leaf stuck to the rim, and the sages at the river feel full.

games.q: all you have for the home altar today is one banana. by Krishna and the last leaf, is it enough?
o: yes. offered with love, one leaf was enough.
no. an offering has to be a full meal.
only if a priest offers it for you.
games.why: Krishna ate one scrap from an empty pot and the soul of the world was satisfied. in the Gita he says a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, offered with love, is accepted.

practice: At your next meal, before the first bite, set aside a small portion, a spoonful, a piece of fruit, and offer it silently, the way many Hindu families do; then eat it or share it as prasad.

Some families say a short verse from the Gita before eating, brahmarpanam, offering the meal back to God; others simply say Krishna's name. If you don't pray, just pause and thank everyone whose work is on the plate.

wordCard.voice: Draupadi. When the pot was empty and guests were coming, Krishna made a meal of the one leaf on its rim. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, a name later tradition gives the sun's vessel: akshaya, unfailing, and patra, vessel.

carryVoice: Your line: a leaf offered with love is enough for God. Krishna ate the last one. I'll be here tomorrow.
